claims.claim: The drop in input resistance observed during the first two postnatal weeks counteracts the reported increase in IH amplitude, such that sag amplitude and rebound delay remain constant.
claims.source: Our current interpretation is that the drop in input resistance observed during the same timeframe counteracts the reported increase in IH amplitude (Washio et al., 1999), such that sag amplitude and rebound delay remain constant.
claims.evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the data based on biophysical principles.

claims.claim: Previously published studies on SNc dopaminergic neurons have described a monophasic increase in AP amplitude associated with an increase in AP rise slope over the first two postnatal weeks.
claims.source: So far, previously published studies on SNc dopaminergic neurons have described more classical changes in these parameters over the same time range, that is, a monophasic increase in amplitude associated with an increase in AP rise slope (or the subsequent decrease in AP half-width) (Washio et al., 1999; Ferrari et al., 2012), although fewer developmental stages and smaller samples were analyzed compared to the current study.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing AP development.

claims.claim: Previous studies dedicated to mouse cerebral cortex and hippocampus development described a monophasic increase in AP amplitude and acceleration of the AP.
claims.source: Nevertheless, previous studies dedicated to mouse cerebral cortex and hippocampus development described the same type of monophasic increase in amplitude and acceleration of the AP (McCormick and Prince, 1987; Spigelman et al., 1992; Picken Bahrey and Moody, 2003; Williams and Sutherland, 2004).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies from other brain regions for comparison.

claims.claim: The monophasic increase in AP amplitude and acceleration was due to an increase in the amplitude of the transient sodium current over the first two postnatal weeks.
claims.source: One of these studies demonstrated that it was due to an increase in the amplitude of the transient sodium current over the first two postnatal weeks (Picken Bahrey and Moody, 2003), consistent with the role of this current in defining the rise kinetics and the amplitude of the AP (Bean, 2007).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing the mechanism of AP development.

claims.claim: The axon initial segment (AIS), the main site of AP initiation, is located at highly variable distances from the soma (between 0 and 250 µm) in mature SNc dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: For instance, it is known that the axon initial segment (AIS), the main site of AP initiation, is located at highly variable distances from the soma (between 0 and 250 µm) in mature SNc dopaminergic neurons (Hausser et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing AIS location variability.

claims.claim: Mild changes in the location of the AIS can significantly influence the response of the neuron to sensory inputs or current injection.
claims.source: Recent studies have demonstrated that mild changes in the location of the AIS can significantly influence the response of the neuron to sensory inputs (Kuba et al., 2006, 2010) or current injection (Grubb and Burrone, 2010a, 2010b).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies describing the functional significance of AIS location.

claims.claim: Multivariate analyses such as PCA are designed to solve the problem of analyzing many distinct properties that do not co-vary by compressing the number of meaningful parameters.
claims.source: While multivariate analyses such as PCA are designed to solve that problem by compressing the number of meaningful parameters (see next section), we propose an intermediate solution which consists of a visual stacking of the results of the uni-variate analyses performed on each parameter.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the purpose and function of PCA based on established statistical knowledge.

claims.claim: Dimensional stacking entails visualizing a high-dimensional data set in a two-dimensional space and has been recently applied to analyze the electrical behavior of databases of complex realistic neuron models.
claims.source: Dimensional stacking entails visualizing a high-dimensional data set in a two-dimensional space and has been recently applied to analyze the electrical behavior of databases of complex realistic neuron models (Taylor et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that used dimensional stacking.

claims.claim: Multivariate analyses, and in particular clustering analysis, have been mainly used in neurophysiology to classify and distinguish mature neuronal populations.
claims.source: So far, multivariate analyses, and in particular clustering analysis, have been mainly used in neurophysiology to classify and distinguish mature neuronal populations (Ascoli et al., 2008; Karagiannis et al., 2009; McGarry et al., 2010; Laramee et al., 2013; Simonnet et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that used multivariate analyses for neuronal classification.

claims.claim: Research dedicated to the classification of cortical interneuron subpopulations has led to the creation of an international consortium (the Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group).
claims.source: For instance, research dedicated to the classification of cortical interneuron subpopulations (for review see Ascoli et al., 2008; Defelipe et al., 2013) has led to the creation of an international consortium (the Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites reviews describing the classification efforts for cortical interneurons.

claims.claim: Classification of cortical interneurons often relies on the use of hierarchical clustering analysis or similar techniques applied to a combination of morphological, molecular, and electrophysiological criteria.
claims.source: This type of classification often relies on the use of hierarchical clustering analysis or similar techniques applied to a combination of morphological (axon and dendrite length and shape…), molecular (expression of specific genes), and electrophysiological (frequency of spiking, frequency adaptation…) criteria (Karagiannis et al., 2009; Battaglia et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing classification methods for cortical interneurons.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis has been used to analyze the diversity of cortical interneurons or the anatomical differences of cortical principal neurons between different cortical areas.
claims.source: Principal component analysis has also been used to analyze the diversity of cortical interneurons (McGarry et al., 2010) or the anatomical differences of cortical principal neurons between different cortical areas (Laramee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that used PCA for neuronal analysis.

claims.claim: AHC and PCA can be efficiently applied to the analysis of developmental changes in electrical behavior in a given population of neurons.
claims.source: In the current study, we show that AHC and PCA can also be efficiently applied to the analysis of developmental changes in electrical behavior in a given population of neurons.
claims.evidence: The manuscript demonstrates a novel application of multivariate analyses.

claims.claim: The variability in phenotype was decreasing across development.
claims.source: The multi-variate analyses we performed not only revealed that the electrical phenotype of SNc dopaminergic neurons was following a biphasic trajectory, it also revealed that the variability in phenotype was decreasing across development (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents data showing decreasing phenotypic variability.

claims.claim: The observation of decreasing phenotypic variability is consistent with the idea of canalization of development formulated by Conrad Hal Waddington.
claims.source: This observation is particularly interesting and consistent with the idea of canalization of development formulated by the English embryologist Conrad Hal Waddington (Waddington, 1942, 1957; Debat and David, 2001).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites Waddington's theory to interpret the findings.

claims.claim: Waddington postulated that in a canalised system, trajectories starting from any point within a certain volume will converge to a single end point which is the corresponding steady-state.
claims.source: In this theory, Waddington postulated the following, referring in particular to organ development: 'In a canalised system of the kind we have been considering, trajectories starting from any point within a certain volume will converge to a single end point which is the corresponding steady-state…' (Waddington, 1957).
claims.evidence: The manuscript quotes Waddington's theory.

claims.claim: The variability in phenotype (and the corresponding region of the PCA space) is much larger at early developmental stages (P2–P5) than at late developmental stages where all values cluster in a single point of space.
claims.source: This precisely describes what is occurring with SNc dopaminergic neuron's phenotype as defined in the PCA space: the variability in phenotype (and the corresponding region of the PCA space) is much larger at early developmental stages (P2–P5) than at late developmental stages where all values cluster in a single point of space (Figures 9C and 10).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes how the data fit Waddington's theory.

claims.claim: Neurons may be very heterogeneous early in development and then use flexible developmental trajectories to reach a highly 'attractive' mature phenotype.
claims.source: This suggests that neurons may be very heterogeneous early in development and then use flexible developmental trajectories to reach a highly 'attractive' mature phenotype.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers a developmental principle from the data.

claims.claim: Mature neurons generate highly similar patterns of activity using variable solutions of underlying conductances, commonly displaying twofold to fourfold ranges of expression/amplitude of ion channels/currents.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that mature neurons generate highly similar patterns of activity using variable solutions of underlying conductances, commonly displaying twofold to fourfold ranges of expression/amplitude of ion channels/currents (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Schulz et al., 2006, 2007; Goaillard et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2009; Amendola et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing variability in ion channel expression.

claims.claim: Mature SNc dopaminergic neurons can generate regular tonic activity patterns of similar frequencies while displaying substantial differences in the amplitude and gating properties of IA and IH.
claims.source: For instance, mature SNc dopaminergic neurons can generate regular tonic activity patterns of similar frequencies while displaying substantial differences in the amplitude and gating properties of IA and IH (Amendola et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing variability in SNc dopaminergic neurons.

claims.claim: Immature neurons, showing heterogeneous phenotypes, may display even larger variability in their underlying conductances.
claims.source: These findings may imply that immature neurons, showing heterogeneous phenotypes, display even larger variability in their underlying conductances.
claims.evidence: The manuscript infers greater variability in immature neurons from the phenotypic data.

claims.claim: The developmental profiles of ion channel expression rapidly change over the first two postnatal weeks, as has been shown in many systems, including the SNc dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: The developmental profiles of ion channel expression rapidly change over the first two postnatal weeks, as has been shown in many systems (Moody and Bosma, 2005), including the SNc dopaminergic neurons (Washio et al., 1999; Dufour et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing developmental changes in ion channel expression.

claims.claim: Slight differences in the developmental timecourses of neurons would certainly exacerbate the cell-to-cell variability in expression of ion channels already observed in mature neurons, and would reveal even larger ranges of expression of ion channels in immature neurons.
claims.source: Slight differences in the developmental timecourses of neurons (visible only at early developmental stages) would certainly exacerbate the cell-to-cell variability in expression of ion channels already observed in mature neurons, and would reveal even larger ranges of expression of ion channels in immature neurons.
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates about the mechanism underlying greater variability in immature neurons.

claims.claim: The first transition (P3 to P5) involves a dramatic concomitant increase in leak conductance.
claims.source: While the increase in calcium-activated potassium current is involved in both transitions, the first transition (P3 to P5) involves a dramatic concomittant increase in leak conductance whereas the second transition (P9 to P11) may rely on a concomittant increase in fast sodium conductance.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the biophysical mechanisms underlying the first developmental transition based on experimental data.

claims.claim: The second transition (P9 to P11) may rely on a concomitant increase in fast sodium conductance.
claims.source: While the increase in calcium-activated potassium current is involved in both transitions, the first transition (P3 to P5) involves a dramatic concomittant increase in leak conductance whereas the second transition (P9 to P11) may rely on a concomittant increase in fast sodium conductance.
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the biophysical mechanisms underlying the second developmental transition based on experimental data.

claims.claim: Manipulating leak, sodium, and calcium-activated potassium currents quantitatively reproduces the changes in electrical phenotype observed between developmental stages.
claims.source: Although we cannot conclude that these biophysical mechanisms are the only ones involved in these developmental transitions, our experiments demonstrate that manipulating these parameters quantitatively reproduces the changes in electrical phenotype observed between these stages (see Figure 11E).
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that specific manipulations reproduce developmental changes.

results.result: SNc dopaminergic neurons were reliably identified using morphological, anatomical, and electrophysiological criteria, with 100% confirmation by tyrosine hydroxylase immunolabeling (n=121).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 provide converging evidence for reliable neuronal identification. The combination of location, morphology, electrophysiological properties, and post-hoc immunohistochemical confirmation (100% accuracy, n=121) demonstrates rigorous cell identification methodology.

results.result: SNc dopaminergic neurons undergo a developmental transition in firing patterns from bursting (P2-3) to irregular (P5-11) to regular pacemaking (after P12), characterized by a decrease in CVISI from ~130% to <20% while maintaining stable firing frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C10 collectively demonstrate a clear developmental trajectory in firing patterns. The data show stable ISIavg (C4) with decreasing CVISI (C5), empirically-derived thresholds (C7), and quantified proportions of firing types across development (C8-C10). The correlation between CVISI and firing pattern (C6) provides mechanistic insight.

results.result: Passive membrane properties show coordinated developmental changes: Rin decreases while Cm increases symmetrically after P2-3, maintaining constant τm, suggesting membrane surface area expansion with stable leak conductance density.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 present data showing reciprocal changes in Rin and Cm that maintain constant τm. Claim C13 provides a biophysically sound interpretation consistent with the relationship τm = Rin × Cm. The inference about leak conductance density is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Sag amplitude and rebound delay remain constant during postnatal development despite reported increases in IH amplitude, suggesting that decreased input resistance counteracts increased IH current amplitude to maintain stable IH and IA channel density.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C87 present data and interpretation, but the explanation relies on reconciling the current findings with prior literature (C16). The interpretation (C15, C87) is plausible but indirect, as channel density was not directly measured. The constant sag/rebound could reflect multiple compensatory mechanisms.

results.result: Action potential properties show heterogeneous developmental trajectories: AP threshold remains stable, AP decay slope and AHP amplitude change monophasically, while AP amplitude, rise slope, and half-width display biphasic changes (decrease P2-5, increase P8-13), suggesting distinct developmental timecourses for different ion channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 present comprehensive data on AP property development with clear statistical support (Figure 3, Figure 6, Table 1). The biphasic changes in C20-C22 are particularly notable and well-documented. Claim C23 provides a reasonable inference about heterogeneous ion channel development, though direct channel measurements were not performed.

results.result: Membrane excitability parameters show distinct developmental profiles: gain at start (GS) decreases gradually over three weeks, gain at end (GE) decreases mainly P2-5 then stabilizes, resulting in spike frequency adaptation (SFA) index remaining stable until P8-9 then dropping.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 describe coordinated changes in excitability parameters with clear data support (Figure 7, Table 1). The distinct timecourses of GS and GE and their relationship to SFA index are logically consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Statistical stacking analysis reveals two major developmental transitions (P2-3 to P5, and P8-9 to P12-13) separated by periods of relative stability, with the second transition being less sharply defined.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 describe results from the statistical stacking approach (Figure 3). The identification of two transitions with an intervening stable period is supported by the systematic ANOVA analysis across 16 parameters and 14 developmental stages. The characterization of the second transition as less clearly defined (C28) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering (AHC) based on 8 spontaneous activity parameters separates 263 neurons into three classes corresponding to bursting (P3.5), irregular (P7.44), and regular (P17.32) firing patterns, with CVISI, AP half-width, rise/decay slopes, and AHP amplitude as key discriminating parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 describe AHC results with clear methodology and outcomes. The separation into three classes (C30-C31) with specific mean ages (C34) and identification of discriminating parameters (C32-C33) is well-documented in Figure 8. The conclusion that AHC discriminates developmental stages (C35) is supported by the age distribution within classes.

results.result: Principal component analysis (PCA) shows that PC1 and PC2 account for ~94% of variance, with CVISI and AHP contributing mainly to PC1, AP properties contributing to both PCs, and ISIavg/AP threshold showing minor contributions. The three AHC classes cluster in distinct PC1/PC2 regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 describe PCA methodology and results with clear quantification. The variance explained (C36), parameter contributions (C37-C39), and consistency with AHC (C40) are well-documented in Figure 9. The analysis appropriately uses covariance-based PCA and retains components explaining >90% variance.

results.result: PCA reveals a biphasic developmental trajectory with two distinct phases: Phase 1 (P2-3 to P5-11) shows concurrent PC1 and PC2 decrease; Phase 2 (P11-15) shows PC1 decrease with PC2 increase. Electrophysiological maturity is reached by P14-15 with no significant subsequent changes, suggesting heterogeneous ion channel development timecourses.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 describe the biphasic trajectory revealed by PCA with clear documentation in Figure 9C. The identification of two phases with distinct PC dynamics and stabilization by P14-15 is well-supported. Claim C46's inference about heterogeneous ion channel development is reasonable given the distinct parameter contributions to each PC and the biphasic trajectory.

results.result: Phenotypic variability decreases progressively during development, with PC1 standard deviation negatively correlated with age (r=-0.802, p<0.001, n=15), revealing a progressively narrowing biphasic developmental trajectory.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 describe variability analysis with strong statistical support. The negative correlation between PC1 SD and age (C48) is highly significant and provides quantitative evidence for decreasing variability (C47). Figure 10 visualizes this narrowing trajectory effectively. The conclusion (C49) appropriately integrates the variability and trajectory findings.

results.result: Pharmacological manipulation of P8 neurons with apamin (to reduce AHP) and dynamic clamp leak subtraction (to increase Rin) induces electrophysiological regression to P2-3 phenotype, with each manipulation accounting for ~50% of the phenotypic change.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 describe experimental manipulations with clear results documented in Figure 11A-B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1. The quantitative assessment that each manipulation accounts for ~50% of change (C53) is supported by the PCA factor loading analysis. The combination reproduces the P2-3 phenotype, validating the biophysical mechanisms.

results.result: Combined apamin and TTX application to P14-16 neurons induces phenotypic regression to P7, with changes in CVISI and AP properties quantitatively similar (but opposite in sign) to the P7-to-P15 developmental transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 describe experimental manipulations with results documented in Figure 11C-D and Figure 11—figure supplement 1. The quantitative similarity to the natural developmental transition (C55) is supported by PCA factor loading analysis, validating the role of SK currents and sodium currents in the second developmental transition.

results.result: SNc dopaminergic neurons undergo postnatal electrophysiological development involving two major transitions (P3-5 and P9-11), reaching mature regular pacemaking by P15. These transitions can be reproduced by distinct manipulations of leak, sodium, and calcium-activated potassium currents, suggesting heterogeneous ion channel development timecourses.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 provide a comprehensive summary of the main findings. The firing pattern transitions (C56), two developmental transitions (C57), maturity by P15 (C58), and reproducibility by specific manipulations (C59) are all well-supported by the data. The inference about heterogeneous ion channel development (C60) is reasonable given the biphasic trajectory and distinct biophysical mechanisms underlying each transition.

results.result: Phenotypic variability decreases during development, consistent with Waddington's canalization theory: early developmental stages (P2-5) show large variability in PCA space, while late stages cluster tightly, suggesting neurons use flexible trajectories to reach a highly attractive mature phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 integrate the variability findings with developmental theory. The data showing decreasing variability (C100, C103) are well-documented in Figures 9C and 10. The connection to Waddington's theory (C101-C102) provides appropriate theoretical context. The inference about flexible trajectories (C104) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The two developmental transitions involve distinct biophysical mechanisms: the first transition (P3-5) involves increased leak conductance and calcium-activated potassium current, while the second (P9-11) involves increased sodium conductance and calcium-activated potassium current. Manipulating these currents quantitatively reproduces developmental phenotypic changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 synthesize the mechanistic findings from the pharmacology and dynamic clamp experiments. The distinct mechanisms for each transition are supported by the experimental data in Figure 11. Claim C112 appropriately notes that these manipulations reproduce but may not be the only mechanisms involved.

results.result: All recordings were performed under standardized conditions: midbrain slices at 30-32°C with continuous superfusion of oxygenated aCSF containing picrotoxin and kynurenate to block synaptic activity, in compliance with ethical guidelines.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 describe methodological details that are clearly stated in the Materials and methods section. The standardized recording conditions (C71-C72) are appropriate for studying intrinsic properties. Ethical compliance (C70) is properly documented.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that mature SNc dopaminergic neurons display context-dependent firing patterns in vivo (regular, irregular, bursting) associated with dopamine release modulation, with regular tonic activity relying on intrinsic conductances while irregular/bursting patterns require synaptic input. In vitro, mature neurons show regular pacemaking, while immature neurons (P9-16) show irregular firing due to T-type calcium and SK channel activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C69 summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the current findings but represent background knowledge rather than new results from this study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations are consistent with the cited work.

results.result: Prior work shows SNc dopaminergic neurons generate calcium spikes/plateaus between E16-P0 that decrease by P7, and bursting relies on calcium conductances including L-type channels. Dopaminergic projections reach striatum by E16 with refinement continuing to P0, likely involving calcium-dependent mechanisms that may be promoted by early intrinsic bursting.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 cite prior literature appropriately. However, claims C77-C78 are speculative inferences about the functional role of early bursting in projection refinement. While the speculation is reasonable and appropriately qualified ('likely', 'may'), it lacks direct experimental support in either the current study or cited work.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that regular tonic activity in SNc dopaminergic neurons relies on multiple intrinsic conductances (sodium, calcium, potassium, hyperpolarization-activated currents), while SK currents control firing regularity in both juvenile and mature neurons, with SK blockade inducing bursting under specific conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 appropriately summarize prior literature with extensive citations. These claims provide important biophysical context for understanding the mechanisms underlying the developmental transitions observed in the current study. The characterizations are consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: Prior studies show SNc dopaminergic neurons reach morphological maturity by P14, with previous electrophysiological studies describing monophasic increases in AP amplitude and rise slope during development, attributed to increased sodium current amplitude in other brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C88-C90 appropriately cite prior literature. Claim C87 provides an interpretation of the current data in light of prior findings. The contrast between prior monophasic findings and the current biphasic observations (C88) is appropriately noted and provides context for the novelty of the current findings.

results.result: Prior work shows the axon initial segment (AIS) in mature SNc dopaminergic neurons is located at variable distances (0-250 µm) from soma, and recent studies demonstrate that AIS location changes can significantly influence neuronal responses to inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 cite prior literature appropriately. These claims provide context for discussing potential mechanisms underlying the biphasic AP changes observed in the current study, though the manuscript appropriately notes this hypothesis requires further investigation.

results.result: Multivariate analyses (PCA, hierarchical clustering) have been primarily used to classify mature neuronal populations, including extensive work on cortical interneurons. The current study demonstrates these methods can also be efficiently applied to analyze developmental changes in electrical behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 appropriately summarize prior applications of multivariate analyses with relevant citations. Claim C99 correctly identifies the novel application to developmental analysis as a contribution of the current study. This represents an important methodological advance.

results.result: Prior work shows mature neurons generate similar activity patterns using variable ion channel expression (2-4 fold ranges), including in SNc dopaminergic neurons. The current findings of greater phenotypic variability in immature neurons suggest even larger variability in underlying conductances, potentially exacerbated by slight differences in developmental timecourses.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 appropriately cite prior literature on degeneracy in mature neurons. Claims C107-C109 make reasonable inferences about immature neurons based on the phenotypic variability data, but these inferences are speculative as ion channel expression was not directly measured. The speculation is appropriately qualified but lacks direct experimental support.
